days.title: Elephants, Wat Ban Den and Mon Cham sunset
days.summary: A morning watching rescued elephants at Elephant Nature Park in the Mae Taeng valley, then a hired car north to the glittering hillside temple of Wat Ban Den and up into the Mae Rim hills for sunset over the terraces of Mon Cham. A long, varied day out of the city — book the elephant visit and the driver in advance.
notes: Changed: all four planned stops do not fit in one day with a standard elephant half-day, because ethical sanctuaries include their own transport and return you to town around 13:30–14:00 (no self-drive drop-ins). Default plan: Elephant Nature Park morning → driver from 14:00 → Wat Ban Den [8] → Mon Cham sunset [7]; Queen Sirikit Botanic Garden [7] is now optional.

To fit all four: ask Elephant Nature Park when booking whether your own driver may collect you at the park at ~13:00 instead of riding their van back (not guaranteed). If yes: ENP → Wat Ban Den (20 min) 13:30–14:30 → Botanic Garden (45 min) 15:15–16:30 → Mon Cham (30 min) 17:00–18:30.
If you prefer nature over temples, swap Wat Ban Den for the Botanic Garden: from town at 14:00 it is 40 min to the garden, then 30 min to Mon Cham — the gentlest version of the day.

Scooter vs driver: a driver (~1,800–2,800 THB / US$50–80 for ~10 h) is the right choice. The day is 130–150 km, the last road up to Mon Cham is steep and twisty, you would ride back down in the dark when it is ~12 °C, and Grab cars are rare up there after sunset. A scooter (~300 THB + fuel) only makes sense for an experienced rider with an IDP motorcycle licence.
Thursday is a weekday: Mon Cham and Wat Ban Den will be quiet (both are packed with Thai visitors at weekends).

stops.name: Ethical elephant half-day: Elephant Nature Park (morning)
stops.description: Elephant Nature Park, founded by Sangduen 'Lek' Chailert in the 1990s, is the best-known rescue sanctuary in Thailand: about 100 elephants, many retired from logging, trekking or street begging, live in a 100+ hectare valley beside the Mae Taeng river with no riding, no shows and no chains. The half-day morning visit drives you 1 h north, then you watch the herds from walkways and the elevated platform, help prepare and hand out fruit from the feeding platform, and walk with a guide who explains each elephant's story; there is a large vegetarian buffet lunch. Guests no longer bathe elephants — if they go to the river, you watch. Ethical alternatives for Thursday: ChangChill (Mae Wang, 1.5 h south-west; strictly observation-only with a guided forest walk, set up with World Animal Protection; half-day morning visits at its Hillside and View Doi sites) — very good but in the opposite direction from Wat Ban Den and Mon Cham. Burm & Emily's (BEES) and Kindred Spirit (both Mae Chaem, 3 h away) are excellent but run only multi-day stays (BEES' one-day walk is Tue/Wed/Fri), so they don't fit.
tips: Book now on elephantnaturepark.org — half-day places sell out weeks ahead in the New Year period. Choose 'Half Day Morning Visit', hotel pick-up.
Wear clothes that can get muddy and closed shoes; bring sunscreen, cash for drinks/souvenirs.

Avoid anything advertised as 'sanctuary' that still includes bathing with elephants, mud spa, or riding: World Animal Protection and Responsible Travel do not support Elephant Jungle Sanctuary, Kanta, Mae Sa, Patara or Chiang Dao elephant camps.
Ask ENP at booking if your driver may collect you at the park at ~13:00 — that unlocks the Botanic Garden as well (see notes).
stops.hours: Half Day Morning: hotel pick-up 07:30–08:00, at the park ~09:00–13:00, back in town ~14:00. Operates daily incl. Thursday.
stops.cost: Elephant Nature Park half day 2,500 THB (~US$73) incl. transport, lunch, guide. ChangChill half day ~US$65–90 via resellers (book direct via changchill.com / WhatsApp +66 86 329 3380).
stops.from_previous: ENP minivan from your hotel, ~1 h

stops.warning: Booking needed now (sells out over New Year). Default ENP transfers return you to town; ask whether a private driver may collect you at the park.

stops.name: Wat Ban Den (Wat Den Salee Sri Muang Gan)
stops.description: Wat Ban Den is a sprawling hillside complex near Mae Taeng built since the 1990s by the revered abbot Kruba Thueang Natsilo, entirely in lavish Lanna style. Dozens of white-and-gold halls, multi-tiered roofs, naga staircases, a huge mirror-mosaic ubosot and twelve chedis — one for each year of the Chinese zodiac, where Thais pray at the one for their birth year — spread over terraces with the hills behind. Some buildings are still under construction, which is part of the charm: you can see wood-carvers and gilders at work. It is free, rarely crowded with foreigners, and the late-afternoon light on the gold is beautiful.
tips: Ask the driver to park at the main (upper) car park and walk downhill through the complex.
Find your own zodiac chedi; a small donation buys a flag or flowers to place there.
Cover shoulders and knees; sarongs can be borrowed at the entrance.
stops.from_previous: Driver collects you at your hotel/ENP office ~14:00; 45 km / ~50 min north on Route 107 (or 20 min from ENP if collected at the park)

video.title: Wat Ban Den, Chiang Mai, Thailand: Exploring a Magnificent Temple World

stops.name: Queen Sirikit Botanic Garden & canopy walkway
stops.description: Thailand's leading botanic garden covers about 1,000 hectares of forested hills in the Mae Sa valley, founded in 1993 and named after Queen Sirikit. The highlight is the Canopy Walkway, a ~400 m steel walkway up to 20 m above the forest floor, with a glass-floored section and views across the valley to Doi Suthep–Pui. Below it, a cluster of glasshouses holds orchids, lotus and water plants, desert plants and a tropical rainforest house with a waterfall. The grounds are hilly and spread out, so you drive between areas.
tips: Go straight to the Canopy Walkway (signposted 'Canopy Walkway / Glasshouse Complex'), then the glasshouses right next to it.
Cars pay 100 THB to drive inside — worth it, as walking between areas takes long.
Be at the canopy walk by ~15:45; staff start closing areas from ~16:30.
stops.cost: 100 THB (~US$3) foreign adult; car 100 THB, scooter 30 THB
stops.from_previous: From Wat Ban Den by car, ~35 km / 45 min via Mae Rim and Route 1096 (from town directly: 27 km / 40 min)

video.title: Queen Sirikit Botanic Garden (Chiang Mai) สวนพฤกษศาสตร์สมเด็จพระนางเจ้าสิริกิติ์ [4K, no commentary]

stops.name: Mon Cham (Mon Jam) sunset
stops.description: Mon Cham is a ridge at about 1,300 m above the Mae Sa valley where Hmong farmers of the Nong Hoi Royal Project grow flowers, strawberries and vegetables on terraces. Small bamboo viewing platforms, cafés and tent pitches are scattered along the crest, looking west and south over layers of hills; at sunset the valleys fill with blue haze and on cold mornings with mist. On a weekday in January it is calm; weekends bring crowds of Thai campers. Have a hot drink and a simple dinner (grilled meats, hot pot) at one of the cafés before the drive down.
tips: Walk to the far end of the ridge, past the first cafés, for the quietest terraces facing west.
Bring a warm layer: it is ~10 °C cooler than town after sunset.
Leave by ~18:45 so the driver tackles the steep upper road soon after dark; back in town ~20:00.
stops.from_previous: By car ~45 km / 1h10 from Wat Ban Den via Mae Rim and the Mae Sa road (Route 1096), last 6 km steep; from the Botanic Garden 15 km / 30 min

video.title: PERFECT Day Trip From Chiang Mai: Mon Jam (Flower Fields, Jungle Coaster & More!)

stops.warning: Steep road; go by car with driver rather than scooter after dark.

days.title: Monk's Trail, Doi Suthep and a night on Doi Pui
days.summary: Hike from the edge of the city up through the forest on the Monk's Trail to the moss-covered temple of Wat Pha Lat and on to Wat Phra That Doi Suthep, the city's holy mountain temple. Ride up past Bhubing Palace to the Hmong village of Doi Pui, and finish at the national park campground near the 1,685 m summit, with the lights of Chiang Mai below.
notes: Camping is legal only at the national park's designated campgrounds. The right one for 'camp at the peak' is the Doi Pui Campground (Lan Kang Tent Doi Pui, ~1,500 m), 3.8 km up a side road north of Bhubing Palace; the other, Montha Than Waterfall campsite, is low on the mountain.

Pack light for the hike: rent the tent and sleeping bag at the campground, carry only warm clothes (night ~5–12 °C), headlamp, water, cash. Leave main bags at the hotel (keep the room or ask them to store bags for one night).

Bhubing Palace is usually closed to visitors when the royal family is in residence (often January–March). Check the same morning (ask your hotel to phone, or ask the songthaew drivers at Doi Suthep, who know); if closed, spend the time in the Hmong village or on the Doi Pui summit trail.
Since 1 Oct 2025 the national park charges foreigners 100 THB at the Pha Lat trail and at Doi Pui; keep your receipt and ask whether it covers the other checkpoint the same day.
If you'd rather not hike the steep upper section (Wat Pha Lat → Doi Suthep, 1–1.5 h), walk back down from Wat Pha Lat and take a songthaew from the zoo instead.

stops.name: Monk's Trail to Wat Pha Lat (and on up to Doi Suthep)
stops.description: The Monk's Trail is the old forest path monks used to walk from the city to Doi Suthep before the road was built in 1935. From the trailhead at the end of Suthep Road, next to the Army TV station, an easy-to-moderate 1.5 km climb (about 45 min, 160 m up) under dipterocarp forest brings you to Wat Pha Lat, a small 14th-century hermitage beside a waterfall-fed stream, with mossy stone stairs, naga guardians, a Burmese-style chedi and a terrace looking out over the city. The upper section continues across the main road and climbs steeply another ~2 km (1–1.5 h, about 500 m up, roots and loose soil) to Wat Phra That Doi Suthep. Early morning is cool, quiet and often misty; monks still use the temple as a meditation retreat, so keep voices low.
tips: Grab to 'Wat Pha Lat Hike (Monk's Trail)' trailhead (~100–150 THB from the old city); if the access road is closed, walk the last ~350 m.
Follow the saffron/coloured banners; at Wat Pha Lat, the upper trail starts on the far side of the main road a few metres uphill.
Download an offline map (Mapy.com or Maps.me) — the upper section is poorly marked.
Wear real shoes, carry 1.5 L water; it's dry and slippery with dust and leaves in January.
stops.hours: Trail open daylight hours (park checkpoint ~06:00–18:00); Wat Pha Lat ~06:00–18:00
stops.cost: Park fee 100 THB (~US$3) for foreigners at the Pha Lat trail since Oct 2025; Wat Pha Lat free
stops.from_previous: Grab from the old city ~15 min, ~100–150 THB

video.title: Hiking the Monk's Trail to Wat Pha Lat in Chiang Mai, Thailand

stops.name: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep
stops.description: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep was founded in 1383 when, according to legend, a white elephant carrying a relic of the Buddha climbed the mountain, trumpeted three times and died on this spot. A 306-step staircase flanked by long naga serpents (or a small funicular) leads up to a cloister around the gleaming gold-plated chedi, surrounded by gilded umbrellas, bells and Buddha images; pilgrims walk around it three times clockwise with lotus buds. From the terrace at 1,050 m you look over the whole Chiang Mai valley. Arriving from the forest trail, before the mid-day tour groups, is the best way to see it.
tips: The upper Monk's Trail comes out on the road just below the temple; walk uphill to the naga staircase.
Shoes off at the upper terrace; cover shoulders/knees (sarongs to borrow).
Coffee and lunch at the stalls along the stairs or the cafés by the car park; this is also where songthaews to Bhubing and Doi Pui leave.
stops.from_previous: On foot: upper Monk's Trail from Wat Pha Lat, ~2 km steep, 1–1.5 h

video.title: Walking Wat Phra That Doi Suthep Thailand 🇹🇭 | Stunning Chiang Mai Temple in 4K

stops.name: Bhubing Palace (Phu Phing Rajanives) gardens
stops.description: Bhubing Palace, built in 1961, is the royal family's winter residence and guesthouse for state visitors, 4 km above Doi Suthep at about 1,300 m. Visitors can't enter the buildings but walk through its gardens: rose gardens (at their best in the cool season), a reservoir lined with royal ferns, coffee bushes, a bamboo grove and a fountain garden, with cool pine-scented air. It is a calm, well-kept park rather than a palace visit, and a pleasant lunch-time stroll on the way up the mountain.
tips: Strict dress code: women must wear a long skirt (sarongs for hire at the gate), no shorts, no sleeveless tops.
Last tickets ~15:30.
If closed, take the songthaew straight on to Doi Pui Hmong village.
stops.hours: Normally daily 08:30–16:30 (tickets until 15:30); usually closed when the royal family is in residence (often January–March)
stops.from_previous: Red songthaew from the Doi Suthep car park, 4 km / 10 min, ~40–60 THB shared (charter ~200–300 THB)
stops.warning: Often closed to visitors in January when the royal family is in residence — check the same morning.

stops.name: Doi Pui Hmong village and summit trail
stops.description: Ban Mong Doi Pui is a Hmong hill-tribe village about 4 km past the palace, settled in the 1950s–60s, whose people once grew opium and now live from flowers, coffee, embroidery and tourism. A lane of stalls with indigo batik and embroidered textiles leads up to a terraced flower garden at the top of the village and a small Hilltribe Opium Museum about Hmong life. From the campground, an easy forest trail (~30 min) leads to the 1,685 m summit of Doi Pui, the highest point of the park, and on a few minutes to the Doi Hua Mu viewpoint with views over the range. Do the summit walk in the late afternoon after checking in at the campground.
tips: Skip the lower souvenir lane quickly and climb to the flower garden (~10–20 THB) for the views.
Village songthaews stop here; there is no regular service the last 3.8 km to the campground — charter one (~200–300 THB) or walk up (about 1 h).
The summit itself is forested; the view is from Doi Hua Mu viewpoint just beyond it.
stops.hours: Village and garden ~08:00–17:00; summit trail daylight only
stops.cost: Village garden ~10–20 THB; park fee 100 THB (Doi Pui checkpoint, if not already paid)
stops.from_previous: Red songthaew from Bhubing Palace, ~4 km / 10 min, ~30–50 THB shared (or charter)

video.title: Doi Pui Hmong Tribal Village Walking Tour in 4K | Chiang Mai Cultural & Mountain Adventure| Thailand

stops.name: Night at Doi Pui Campground (national park)
stops.description: The Doi Pui Campground is a national park camping ground on a grassy slope near the summit at about 1,500 m, with five zones for up to ~100 tents, toilets and showers, a small visitor centre and a restaurant/shop. Thai families come here for the cold air, the sea of city lights after dark and sunrise over the valley. You rent everything on the spot: tents for 2–3 people, sleeping bags, mats and blankets. On a Friday night it is lively but not full; Saturday nights and holidays are the busy ones.
tips: Rent a tent 'with all accessories' (405 THB) and an extra blanket or sleeping bag — nights in January can drop to ~5–10 °C.

Booking: the park's online system (DNP) has been unreliable in 2026; call the campground 086-196-4285 or park office 053-210-244 (ask a Thai-speaking hotel receptionist to help). Walk-ins on a Friday in January are usually fine.
The restaurant closes early (~19:00–20:00); bring snacks, water and a headlamp.
Ask the restaurant staff or a songthaew driver for a phone number to arrange your ride down in the morning.
stops.hours: Campground staffed ~08:30–16:30 (check in before 16:30); overnight stay
stops.cost: Camping fee 30 THB pp/night; tent 2–3 pers. 225 THB, with all accessories 405 THB; sleeping bag/mat from 60 THB; park entry 100 THB foreigners (~US$3)
stops.from_previous: Charter songthaew from Doi Pui village / Bhubing junction ~3.8 km / 10 min (~200–300 THB), or walk ~1 h uphill

video.title: ดอยปุย กางเต็นท์ 1คืน บรรยากาศปลายฝนต้นหนาว Doi Pui Camping in November 2026

stops.warning: Call ahead if possible (086-196-4285); check-in before 16:30.

days.title: Sunrise on the mountain, south-west temples, Saturday walking street
days.summary: Wake up above the clouds for sunrise, ride a red truck down the mountain, and spend the morning at the hilltop temple of Doi Kham and the royal gardens of Rajapruek. After a shower and rest, cycle out to the forest tunnels of Wat Umong and the white chedis of Wat Suan Dok, then end at the silver temple and the Saturday night market on Wua Lai Road.
notes: Changed: Wat Sri Suphan (Silver Temple) moved here from CM1 — it stays open until ~23:00 on Saturdays and stands inside the Wua Lai walking street.
Changed: after Rajapruek go back to the hotel for a shower and to pick up a bicycle — the bike part (Umong, Suan Dok) starts from the old city.
What to cut if tired after the camping night: Royal Park Rajapruek first (it's the least special), then Wat Suan Dok. Keep Wat Umong and the evening.
Saturday crowds: Doi Kham and Wat Umong are busier with Thai visitors at weekends; go early to Doi Kham.

stops.name: Sunrise over Chiang Mai from Doi Pui
stops.description: From the campground's east-facing slope the sun comes up at about 06:55 over the Chiang Mai valley, often above a layer of mist with the city lights still shining below. In January the cold, dry air gives the clearest mornings of the year. For a wilder view, walk 25–30 min in the dark up the summit trail to the Doi Hua Mu viewpoint. Have a hot coffee from the campground shop and pack up.
tips: Be outside by 06:20: the sky colours start ~30 min before sunrise.
Wear everything warm you have; it is often 5–10 °C with wind.
Return rented gear to the office by ~08:00.
stops.from_previous: Out of your tent
stops.image_credit: SUTHATCMU, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ลมหายใจแห่งป่าดอยสุเทพ.jpg

stops.name: Down the mountain by red songthaew
stops.description: The red songthaews (rot daeng, 'red car') are Chiang Mai's shared pick-up trucks with two benches in the back. Shared trucks run between the Chiang Mai Zoo / CMU gate, Doi Suthep, Bhubing and Doi Pui village and leave when ~8–10 seats are filled — in the early morning they mostly come up, not down, so going down from the campground needs a little planning. Easiest: arrange the evening before (via the campground restaurant or the driver who brought you) a red truck to pick you up at ~08:00 and take you straight down the mountain to Doi Kham, ~25 km / 50 min. Budget option: walk down 3.8 km to the Doi Pui village junction (~45 min) and catch a shared truck to the zoo (~90 THB), then Grab to Doi Kham (~150–200 THB).
tips: Agree the price for the whole truck before getting in (~600–900 THB to Doi Kham or the old city; cheaper if other campers share).
Grab cars will usually accept a pick-up at Doi Suthep temple car park, rarely at the campground.
If you'd rather go to the hotel first, the charter to the old city is similar in price; then do Doi Kham by Grab.
stops.cost: Charter ~600–900 THB (US$18–26) per truck; shared ~40–90 THB pp
stops.from_previous: Pre-arranged songthaew pick-up at the campground

stops.name: Wat Phra That Doi Kham
stops.description: Wat Phra That Doi Kham ('temple of the golden mountain') sits on a small hill south-west of the city and is said to date from 687, the time of the Haripunchai kingdom, making it older than Chiang Mai itself. Its gold chedi is surrounded by a big white seated Buddha about 17 m high, which looks out over the airport, the city and Doi Suthep behind. Thais come here to make wishes and, when they come true, return to offer jasmine garlands — you will see thousands of them hanging around the Buddha. It is quieter and more local than Doi Suthep.
tips: Drive up to the top car park (the staircase from the bottom has ~300 steps).
Look for the jasmine garland sellers at the steps — buying one to offer is a nice gesture (~20 THB).
Morning light is behind you when looking at the big Buddha.
stops.cost: ~30 THB (~US$1) foreigners (some visitors report free entry; donations welcome)
stops.from_previous: Songthaew charter down the mountain, ~25 km / 50 min (or Grab from the zoo ~20 min, ~150–200 THB)

video.title: WAT PHRA THAT DOI KHAM (Temple of the Golden Mountain): Chiang Mai, Thailand (4K)

stops.name: Royal Park Rajapruek
stops.description: Royal Park Rajapruek was created for the 2006 International Horticultural Exposition marking King Bhumibol's 60 years on the throne and is now an 80-hectare botanical park at the foot of Doi Suthep. Its centrepiece is Ho Kham Luang, a huge pavilion in classic Lanna temple architecture with gilded roofs and fine wood carving, set behind a lotus pond. Around it are themed gardens donated by different countries, an orchid house, a bougainvillea tunnel and a tropical greenhouse, all at their freshest in the cool season. It is open, sunny and well kept — a calm walk after the camping night.
tips: Take the hop-on tram (around 20 THB or included) to the far gardens and walk back to Ho Kham Luang.
Best photo of Ho Kham Luang: from across the reflecting pond in front.
Little shade between gardens: hat and water.
stops.from_previous: Grab from Doi Kham ~2 km / 5 min (~60–80 THB) — they are neighbours

video.title: Royal Park Rajapruek 👑 | Chiang Mai Thailand | [4K 60 FPS HDR]

stops.name: Wat Umong (by bike)
stops.description: Wat Umong Suan Puthatham is a forest temple at the foot of Doi Suthep, founded by King Mangrai in the late 13th century for a monk who liked to meditate in the woods. Its unique feature is a set of brick tunnels (umong) built under a large mound in the 1300s, with Buddha images in niches and traces of old murals, under a ruined chedi you can climb behind. Around it are big trees hung with signs of Buddhist proverbs ('talking trees'), a pond with fish and turtles, an emaciated 'fasting Buddha' statue and a broken Buddha garden. It is still an active meditation centre and feels peaceful even at weekends.
tips: Cycle via the quiet Suthep Road / CMU side lanes rather than the busy Canal Road.
Shoes off before the tunnels; they are dim and cool.
Buy fish food at the pond (10 THB) for the turtles; walk the forest loop behind the chedi.
stops.from_previous: Grab back to the hotel after Rajapruek (~20 min, ~150 THB), rest, then bicycle from the old city ~5 km / 25 min (bike rental ~50–100 THB/day)

video.title: CHIANG MAI - Underground tunnel Temple - Wat Umong

stops.name: Wat Suan Dok
stops.description: Wat Suan Dok ('flower garden temple') was built in 1370 by King Kuena in his royal flower garden for a visiting Sukhothai monk. A field of brilliant white chedis holds the ashes of Chiang Mai's royal family, set around a large bell-shaped gold chedi containing a relic of the Buddha. The big open-sided wihan holds a 500-year-old bronze Buddha, and the temple also houses a campus of the Buddhist monastic university. Late afternoon light on the white chedis, with Doi Suthep behind, is the classic view.
tips: Best photo: from the west side of the white chedi field with Doi Suthep in the background (late afternoon).
Monk chat runs here only Mon/Wed/Fri 17:00–19:00 — not on Saturday.
Short ride (2 km) back along Suthep Road towards the old city.
stops.from_previous: Bicycle ~2 km / 10 min east along Suthep Road

stops.name: Wat Sri Suphan (Silver Temple)
stops.description: Wat Sri Suphan, founded in 1500, is the temple of the Wua Lai silversmiths' quarter, whose craftsmen came from Burma-ruled villages two centuries ago. Since 2004 the community has covered its ordination hall (ubosot) inside and out in hand-hammered silver and aluminium panels showing Buddhist stories, Lanna patterns and even a few cartoon characters. At dusk the panels catch the light, and on Saturday evenings the temple is lit up and open late while the walking street runs past its gate. Silversmiths often work in the open workshop in the grounds.
tips: Only men may enter the silver ubosot (it is an active ordination hall with relics buried underneath); women can see it from outside and visit the rest of the grounds, the wihan and the workshop.
Arrive before 18:00 to see it in daylight and then lit up.
Some evenings there is a free meditation/monk chat session — ask at the gate.
stops.from_previous: Bicycle back into the old city and out through Chiang Mai Gate, ~3 km / 15 min (return the bike or leave it at the hotel)
stops.image_credit: Michael Jenselius from Chiang Mai, Thailand, CC BY 2.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wat_Si_Suphan,_Chiang_Mai.jpg

video.title: 【4K Stroll】Wat Sri Suphan - Chiang Mai - Thailand / The World's First Silver Temple

stops.warning: Men only inside the silver ordination hall.

stops.name: Wua Lai Saturday Walking Street
stops.description: Every Saturday evening Wua Lai Road, the old silversmiths' street running south from Chiang Mai Gate, closes to traffic for about 1 km and fills with stalls. It is smaller and more local than the famous Sunday market: silver jewellery and bowls from the street's own workshops, handmade crafts, clothes, and lots of food — grilled river fish, sai ua sausage, khanom krok coconut cakes, fresh juices. Temples along the street (Wat Sri Suphan, Wat Muen San) open their grounds as food courts with tables. Street musicians, many of them blind or students, play along the way.
tips: Walk the full length from Chiang Mai Gate south and back; food courts inside temple grounds are the best places to sit.
Peak crush is 19:00–20:30; it thins after 21:00.
Bargain gently on crafts; food prices are fixed.
stops.from_previous: Wat Sri Suphan is on Wua Lai Road, 1 min walk

video.title: Chiang Mai Night Market 4K Walk | Wua Lai Saturday Walking Street, Thailand Walkthrough

days.title: Coconut Market, ancient-tree park, fly to Siem Reap
days.summary: A slow last morning north of the city: breakfast among the palms at the weekend Coconut Market, then the new Changthong Heritage Park, a garden of rescued ancient trees. Collect your bags and fly out at midday via Bangkok to Siem Reap.
notes: Identified: 'Changthong Heritage Park' is a privately created park of rescued ancient and rare trees in San Phi Suea, ~8 km north of the old city, opened in November 2024. It is ~5.5 km (12 min) north of the Coconut Market, so the two pair well.

Timing depends on your flight: with a ~12:00–13:00 departure from Chiang Mai, do the market at 07:30 and the park at opening (09:30), and leave the park by 10:45. With a later flight (14:00+), you can relax both visits.
If the flight is earlier than 11:30, skip Changthong and do only the Coconut Market.

stops.name: Coconut Market (Talad Maprao), Fa Ham
stops.description: The Coconut Market is a weekend morning market held in an old coconut plantation in Fa Ham, about 5 km north-east of the old city. Stalls of local food, coffee and crafts line a narrow canal between rows of tall palms, with bamboo platforms to sit on, live acoustic music and a small farm corner with goats. It is a relaxed, photogenic place for breakfast: khao soi, grilled pork and sticky rice, khanom krok, fresh coconut water and coconut ice cream served in the shell. Mostly Thai visitors; get there early before it gets busy and hot.
tips: Come as it opens: soft light through the palms and no crowds before ~09:30.
Try 'burnt' (roasted) coconut water and coconut ice cream.
Cash only at most stalls; songthaews and Grab drop off at the soi entrance.
stops.hours: Fri–Sun ~07:00/08:00–14:00/15:00 (sources vary; vendors pack up from ~13:30); open Sunday 10 Jan
stops.from_previous: Grab from the old city ~6 km / 15 min (~100–130 THB)

video.title: Hidden Market in Chiang Mai, Thailand | Coconut Market | 4K Walking Tour

stops.name: Changthong Heritage Park (ancient-tree park)
stops.description: Changthong Heritage Park is a 12-hectare 'museum without walls' of living trees created by landscape designer Bunrak Thanacharoenrot, who spent 25 years finding and transplanting more than 2,000 old and rare trees from northern Thailand — some bought from farmers, others saved from construction sites. A winding path leads through themed areas such as the Blackwood Tunnel and Red Trunk Tunnel, a mossy 'Forest Heart' cascade, a cycad grove and a lake ringed by coconut palms with twisted and split trunks; some trees are thought to be 400–500 years old. Trees are labelled in Thai and English, and misters create a cool, misty atmosphere. It opened in November 2024 and is still little known among foreign visitors.
tips: Arrive at opening (09:30) for the quietest paths and the mist.
Allow 1–1.5 h for a loop; there is a café on site.
Ask the Grab driver to wait or book the next one to the airport before you leave (~13 km / 25 min).
stops.from_previous: Grab from the Coconut Market ~5.5 km / 12 min (~90–120 THB)

stops.name: Fly Chiang Mai → Siem Reap (via Bangkok)
stops.description: There is no direct flight from Chiang Mai to Siem Reap: you connect in Bangkok. Recommended: one booking on Bangkok Airways (e.g. PG 224 CNX 12:10 → BKK 13:35, then PG 907 BKK 17:25 → SAI ~18:45), or Thai AirAsia via Don Mueang (e.g. CNX ~11:30 → DMK 12:45, then FD 614 DMK 15:50 → SAI 16:55). See 'transport_out' for all options, prices and the Cambodian entry paperwork. Siem Reap Angkor International (SAI) is ~50 km from town: shuttle bus ~US$8 or taxi ~US$30–35, 50–60 min.
tips: Pick up your bags at the hotel on the way: Changthong → old city → airport is ~35 min in total.
Be at CNX 1h30 before departure (international connections check in at domestic counters).
Fill in the Cambodia e-Arrival card online (free) within 7 days before arrival.
stops.cost: Grab Changthong → airport ~200–250 THB; flights ~4,000–9,000 THB (US$115–260) one way, see transport_out
stops.from_previous: Grab from Changthong ~13 km / 25–35 min (via hotel for bags)
stops.warning: Book flights now: Sunday connections via Bangkok are limited.

extras.name: Chiang Rai: White Temple, Blue Temple, Black House (day trip or 1 night)
extras.description: Chiang Rai, 180 km north-east of Chiang Mai, is home to three modern art temples unlike anything else in Thailand. Wat Rong Khun (the White Temple), begun in 1997 by artist Chalermchai Kositpipat, is an all-white fantasy of mirror mosaics reached across a bridge over a pit of reaching hands, with murals inside mixing Buddhist hell with pop culture. Wat Rong Suea Ten (the Blue Temple, 2016) glows sapphire and gold around a white Buddha, and Baan Dam (the Black House) is artist Thawan Duchanee's eerie complex of ~40 dark teak buildings filled with horns, skulls and animal skins. Add the giant white Guanyin of Wat Huay Pla Kang on a hill north of town. Day trip: leave at 07:00 by private car (3–3.5 h each way; ~3,500–4,500 THB / US$100–130 for the day) → White Temple ~10:00 (it is on the way, 13 km south of town) → lunch → Blue Temple → Baan Dam → Wat Huay Pla Kang → back in Chiang Mai ~20:30 (about 7 h of driving, a long day). One night (better): Green Bus from Chiang Mai Arcade terminal (~3–3.5 h, ~200–300 THB, frequent from ~06:30) → afternoon Blue Temple and Baan Dam, evening Clock Tower light show and night bazaar (or the Saturday walking street) → next morning White Temple at 08:00 and Wat Huay Pla Kang, then the bus back, or continue to Doi Mae Salong or Phu Chi Fa. You could also fly out from Chiang Rai (CEI) via Bangkok Don Mueang to Siem Reap instead of returning to Chiang Mai.
tips: Be at the White Temple at opening (08:00): tour buses from Chiang Mai arrive ~10:30–11:00.
The White Temple fee for foreigners doubled to 200 THB from 1 Jan 2026 (includes the art gallery); the Blue Temple is free; Baan Dam ~80 THB.
The Clock Tower in town (also by Chalermchai) has a light-and-music show at 19:00, 20:00 and 21:00.
extras.hours: White Temple daily 08:00–17:30 (last entry ~17:00); Blue Temple ~07:00–20:00; Baan Dam ~09:00–17:00
extras.cost: White Temple 200 THB (~US$6); Baan Dam ~80 THB; Blue Temple free; bus 200–300 THB each way; private car 3,500–4,500 THB/day
extras.from_previous: Green Bus from Chiang Mai Arcade Bus Terminal 2, ~3–3.5 h; or private car

extras.what_to_swap: Best with an extra (17th) night: insert it as a full day after CM4 and fly to Siem Reap on Mon 11 Jan (or take the night from Siem Reap). Within 16 nights: as a day trip it replaces CM2 (elephants/Mae Rim); as one night (Sat→Sun) it replaces the CM4 afternoon, the Wua Lai market and the Sunday morning, and you fly to Siem Reap from Chiang Rai (CEI → DMK → SAI) instead.
extras.rating_note: exciting, but far. If i end up having on the higher end for number of days, I'll add. In general, worth adding to our final writeup in case I have extra time.

extras.name: Sukhothai & Si Satchanalai (1 night between Bangkok and Chiang Mai)
extras.description: Sukhothai ('dawn of happiness') was the capital of the first great Thai kingdom from about 1238 to 1438, the period that produced the Thai alphabet and the graceful 'walking Buddha' style. The UNESCO-listed historical park, 12 km west of the modern town, spreads ~190 ruins across moated lawns and lotus ponds that you explore by bicycle: Wat Mahathat with its lotus-bud chedi and rows of standing Buddhas, the Khmer-style towers of Wat Si Sawai, Wat Sa Si on its island, and outside the walls the giant seated Buddha peering through a slit in the walls of Wat Si Chum. Si Satchanalai, 55 km north, was Sukhothai's twin city: a quieter, forested park beside the Yom river, with Wat Chang Lom's chedi ringed by 39 elephant sculptures and very few visitors. Sunset and sunrise at Wat Mahathat, reflected in the ponds, are the highlights. From Bangkok: Bangkok Airways flies BKK → Sukhothai (THS) about once or twice a day (~1h10, ~2,500–4,000 THB; the airport is ~30 km from town, with an airline shuttle); or bus from Mo Chit (Transport Co., Win Tour, Phitsanulok Yanyon) ~6–7 h, ~350–450 THB; or train to Phitsanulok (5–6 h) and a 1 h bus. Onward to Chiang Mai: buses from Sukhothai bus terminal (Win Tour, Green Bus) take ~5–5.5 h, ~250–320 THB, with several departures from morning to early afternoon. Suggested plan: Wed 6 Jan fly or bus to Sukhothai, afternoon by bike in the central zone and sunset at Wat Mahathat; Thu 7 Jan sunrise, Wat Si Chum by bike, then either Si Satchanalai by hired car (~1 h each way) or the late-morning bus to Chiang Mai, arriving early evening.
tips: Stay in Old Sukhothai (next to the park), not the new town, so you can cycle in at sunrise.
Rent a bicycle opposite the central-zone gate (~30–50 THB): the central zone is flat and the outer zones are 1–3 km apart.
Each zone has its own ticket (~100 THB each).
extras.hours: Sukhothai central zone ~06:30–19:30 (outer zones ~07:30–17:30); Si Satchanalai ~08:00–17:00
extras.cost: ~100 THB (~US$3) per zone plus ~10–50 THB per bike/car; Si Satchanalai 100 THB
extras.from_previous: From Bangkok: flight 1h10 or bus 6–7 h; on to Chiang Mai: bus 5–5.5 h

video.title: SUKHOTHAI: Ancient Kingdom of Thailand! (4K)

extras.what_to_swap: Replaces the Wed 6 Jan Bangkok → Chiang Mai flight and CM1: you arrive in Chiang Mai on Thu 7 Jan evening. Do the old city and Wat Chedi Luang by night that evening and drop CM2 (elephants/Mae Rim) — the cost is one Chiang Mai day.

extras.name: Lampang: Wat Phra That Lampang Luang & horse carts
extras.description: Lampang, 100 km south-east of Chiang Mai, is a calm provincial town known for teak mansions, Burmese-style temples and the horse-drawn carriages that still carry visitors around. Its great sight is Wat Phra That Lampang Luang, 18 km outside town: a walled 13th–15th-century hilltop temple, perhaps the finest surviving Lanna wooden temple, where a pinhole in a dark hall projects an upside-down image of the gold chedi. In town see Baan Sao Nak (a teak house on 116 pillars) and Wat Si Rong Muang (Burmese teak), and walk the riverside Kad Kong Ta street (walking street on weekend evenings). The traveler already ruled out Wat Chaloem Phra Kiat (the cliff-top chedis), which is a separate trip.
tips: Train from Chiang Mai station (~2 h, scenic, a few departures daily) or bus/van (~1.5 h).
Hire a songthaew from Lampang town to Lampang Luang (~400–500 THB return with waiting).
A horse-cart tour of town costs ~300–400 THB for 30–60 min.
extras.hours: Wat Phra That Lampang Luang daily ~07:30–17:00; Baan Sao Nak ~10:00–17:00
extras.cost: Temple free / donation; Baan Sao Nak ~50 THB
extras.from_previous: Train ~2 h or bus ~1.5 h from Chiang Mai

video.title: Lampang | Provinces of Thailand: Travel Guide

extras.what_to_swap: Replaces CM2 or the CM4 afternoon; also fits as a stop on the Sukhothai → Chiang Mai bus route.

extras.name: Doi Mae Salong (Santikhiri)
extras.description: A mountain-top village at ~1,200 m near the Myanmar border, founded by Chinese Kuomintang soldiers who retreated from Yunnan after 1949, now surrounded by oolong tea terraces. Taste tea at plantations such as 101 Tea, eat Yunnanese noodles and dumplings, visit the KMT memorial museum, walk the early-morning market where Akha and Lisu traders sell vegetables, and climb to the Princess Mother's chedi for the view over ranges of hills. January is cold (~5–8 °C at night) and in some years brings cherry blossom. It is ~1.5 h from Chiang Rai (3.5–4 h from Chiang Mai), so it only makes sense combined with a Chiang Rai overnight.
tips: Go up the afternoon before: morning mist over the tea terraces is the reason to stay.
Public transport: bus to Mae Chan, then a yellow songthaew up the mountain (infrequent); a hired car from Chiang Rai is much easier.
extras.cost: Guesthouses ~600–2,000 THB; tea tastings free–100 THB

extras.what_to_swap: Only as part of a 2-night Chiang Rai extension; would replace CM2 and CM4 or needs extra nights.

extras.name: Phu Chi Fa sunrise
extras.description: A knife-edge cliff at ~1,600 m on the Laos border, where at dawn a sea of clouds fills the Mekong valley below you — one of the best sunrise views in Thailand, and December–January is the peak season. You sleep in Phu Chi Fa village or nearby resorts, walk 20–40 min up in the dark with a torch, and watch the sun rise at ~06:45 over the clouds. It is 2–2.5 h from Chiang Rai on winding roads (4.5 h from Chiang Mai), so it needs a car and an overnight; it is very crowded with Thai visitors at weekends.
tips: Go on a weekday and book a room in the village in advance.
Local songthaews shuttle from the village to the start of the path (~30–40 THB) from ~05:00.
Bring gloves and a hat: it can be close to 0–5 °C at dawn.
extras.cost: Free; rooms ~500–1,500 THB; car with driver ~4,000 THB/day

video.title: Phu Chi Fa | Sunrise with sea mist Over Chiang Rai Mountains

extras.what_to_swap: Only with a 2-night Chiang Rai extension. You already have a mountain sunrise on Doi Pui (CM4), so this is lower priority.

cities.name: Siem Reap
cities.tagline: Angkor at sunrise on foot, the grand circuit by bike, and life on the Tonle Sap.
cities.intro: Siem Reap is a relaxed riverside town that exists, these days, as the gateway to Angkor: the remains of the Khmer Empire's capital, spread over some 400 km² of forest and rice fields just to the north. This leg is about seeing the great temples at the quietest times — a walk-in sunrise at Angkor Wat, forest paths between Ta Keo, Ta Prohm and Banteay Kdei, and a long e-bike loop around Angkor Thom and the Grand Circuit. One day off the temples shows the countryside and the stilt-house fishing towns of the Tonle Sap lake. January is the dry, cool peak season, so the plan aims to stay one step ahead of the crowds.

stay.why: Walkable to restaurants, Pub Street, the river path and the airport shuttle stop; tuk-tuks everywhere. Wat Bo (east bank) is quieter with boutique hotels. It is 7–8 km to Angkor Wat.

stay.area: North of town (Charles de Gaulle Blvd / Angkor National Museum)
stay.why: Closest to the temples: makes the walk to Angkor Wat for sunrise 5–6 km instead of 7.5 km, and the e-bike ride shorter. Leafy and quiet, a 10–15 min walk or short tuk-tuk ride to the Old Market.

stay.area: Salakomreuk / Kandal Village (east of the river)
stay.why: Residential lanes with small pool villas and cafés; peaceful but 5–10 min from the centre by tuk-tuk.

cities.arrival: Fly in to Siem Reap Angkor International Airport (SAI), 47 km east of town (there is no direct Chiang Mai flight; connect in Bangkok — BKK with Bangkok Airways/Thai/Cambodia Airways or DMK with Thai AirAsia — and the Thai–Cambodian land border is closed). Before flying: complete Cambodia's free e-Arrival card (arrival.gov.kh, within 7 days before arrival) and ideally the e-Visa (evisa.gov.kh, US$30 + fee); visa on arrival is also available (US$30 cash, photo). Into town: airport shuttle bus about US$8 (60–70 min, ends at CDF Duty Free near Wat Bo; buy at the desk in arrivals), fixed-price taxi about US$25–35 per car (50–60 min), or a hotel pickup US$25–35. Tuk-tuks from the airport take ~90 min (about US$15) and are dusty. ATMs at the airport dispense US dollars.
cities.getting_around: Grab and PassApp work well in town: tuk-tuk (remork) rides cost about US$1–3; choose the larger remork option for luggage. Tuk-tuk day hire: small circuit about US$15–20, Grand Circuit US$20–25, add US$5 for a sunrise start; agree the route and price the evening before. Car with driver to Kompong Khleang about US$35–60. Bicycles rent for about US$3–6 a day and e-bikes for about US$10–15 a day (24 h) from shops around Sivatha Blvd and the Old Market; there is also a 23 km APSARA cycle path through the park (old Charles de Gaulle checkpoint → Prasat Kravan → Banteay Kdei → Ta Keo, and Srah Srang → Pre Rup → Angkor Thom). US dollars are the main currency for anything over a dollar; change comes in riel (about 4,000 riel = US$1).
cities.weather: January is the heart of the dry season: almost no rain, low humidity by Cambodian standards, cool mornings around 20–22°C and afternoons of 30–32°C. Roads and temple paths are dusty. Sunrise is about 06:31 and sunset about 17:55 (first light from about 06:05; dark by about 18:20). Bring sunscreen, a hat and 2–3 litres of water on temple days.
cities.etiquette: Temples: cover shoulders and knees (enforced at Angkor Wat's Bakan, Baphuon's upper level and Phnom Bakheng; no short shorts or vest tops), remove hats in sanctuaries, do not touch or sit on carvings, and do not climb roped-off areas. Monks: women should not touch a monk or hand things directly to one. Drones need a permit. Scams: only buy Angkor passes from the official office, kiosks, app or angkorenterprise.gov.kh; ignore 'free' blessings with red string that end in a donation demand; avoid buying milk powder for begging mothers (it is resold); agree tuk-tuk prices in advance; children selling at temples are often kept out of school, so do not buy from them. Money: US dollars in small, clean, untorn notes; cards work in hotels, better restaurants and the ticket centre, but bring cash for tuk-tuks, boats, markets and the quad ride.
cities.transport_out: Thu 14 Jan, destination not yet chosen. Direct flights from SAI (2026 network): Bangkok Suvarnabhumi (Bangkok Airways, Cambodia Airways, Emirates, Thai Airways seasonal; ~1 h 05, about US$80–150), Bangkok Don Mueang (Thai AirAsia; ~1 h), Kuala Lumpur (AirAsia Cambodia; ~2 h), Singapore (Singapore Airlines; ~2 h), Hanoi (VietJet, Vietnam Airlines; ~1 h 45), Ho Chi Minh City (Vietnam Airlines, Air Cambodia; ~1 h), Da Nang (Air Cambodia), Phnom Penh (Air Cambodia, Cambodia Airways; ~45 min), Luang Prabang (Lao Airlines/Vietnam Airlines, seasonal), Pakse, Dubai (Emirates) and several Chinese cities. By road, Phnom Penh is 5–6 h by bus (Giant Ibis, Mekong Express; about US$15–20) — the land border with Thailand remains closed. Book now: the onward flight (peak season; Bangkok flights are cheapest booked early), and decide whether a midday-or-later departure lets you use the last pass day for a Thursday sunrise. Leave town about 3 h before departure (47 km to SAI).

days.title: Arrival evening: Old Market and the river
days.summary: You land in the late afternoon or evening after connecting in Bangkok, ride about an hour into town, and settle in. Keep it easy: a walk through the Old Market and along the river, dinner, and an early night before the 04:10 start for Angkor Wat sunrise.
notes: Changed: the Chiang Mai → Siem Reap connections land at 16:55 (AirAsia via Don Mueang) or 18:45 (Bangkok Airways via Suvarnabhumi), so there is no time for the ticket counter or a sunset in the park today. Buy the pass online instead, and the balloon moves to an optional sunrise ride on SR4.

Alternative: an early flight (CNX 06:30–08:30, then FD 610 DMK 10:00 → SAI 11:05) gets you here by noon with time for the pass counter and sunset, but skips the Coconut Market and Changthong on Sunday morning.
Angkor pass plan: buy a 3-day pass with Mon 11 Jan as the start date. Holding a ticket dated for tomorrow lets you enter from 16:45 today for sunset, and this evening does not count as a pass day.

Use the 3 pass days on Mon 11 (SR2), Wed 13 (SR4) and either Thu 14 (sunrise before the airport, if your flight leaves after about 12:00) or Tue 12 (only if you swap Kompong Khleang for Phnom Krom sunset, which needs the pass). Kompong Khleang, the museum and the balloon do not need the pass.

stops.name: Arrive at Siem Reap Angkor International Airport (SAI)
stops.description: Siem Reap's new airport (SAI) opened in October 2023, about 47 km east of town, replacing the old airport next to the temples. It is a large, quiet terminal with ATMs (USD), SIM card counters and a fixed-price taxi desk in arrivals. Cambodia issues visas on arrival (US$30, cash, passport photo) or you can get an e-Visa in advance. The road into town runs through flat rice country and takes 50–60 minutes.
tips: Get an e-Visa (evisa.gov.kh) before you fly to skip the visa-on-arrival queue.
Buy a local SIM (Smart, Cellcard or Metfone, about US$5–10 for plenty of data) in arrivals: Grab and PassApp need data.
The cheapest way in is the airport shuttle bus (about US$8, 60–70 min, ends at the CDF Duty Free shop near Wat Bo); the official taxi desk charges about US$25–35 per car; a hotel pickup is US$25–35.
Bring small, clean US dollar notes: torn or old notes are refused, and change under $1 comes back in riel.
stops.hours: Airport open for all flights; shuttle bus timetable from the airport (early 2025): 09:30, 11:00, 12:30, 15:00, 16:00, 17:00, 17:30, 20:00, 21:00, 22:00 — check on arrival
stops.cost: Shuttle US$8 (≈ 32,000 riel); taxi US$25–35; hotel pickup US$25–35
stops.from_previous: Flight from Chiang Mai via Bangkok (BKK with Bangkok Airways/Thai, or DMK with Thai AirAsia); about 4–7 h door to door including the connection

video.title: All You Need To Know To Arrive In Siem Reap Angkor Airport and Get To Town

stops.warning: No direct Chiang Mai–Siem Reap flight; you connect in Bangkok. The Thailand–Cambodia land border is closed.

stops.name: Buy the 3-day Angkor pass (Angkor Ticket Centre, Road 60)
stops.description: All of the Angkor Archaeological Park, plus Roluos, Banteay Srei, Beng Mealea and Phnom Krom, is covered by one pass sold by Angkor Enterprise. The 3-day pass (US$62) covers any 3 days within its validity window (7 days according to the 2026 ticket card; older guides say 10), so the days do not need to be consecutive. Multi-day passes carry your photo, taken by webcam at the counter or uploaded when you buy online. The counters are a large hall on Road 60, about 4 km north-east of the Old Market, on the way to the temples.
tips: After 16:45 you can buy a pass dated for tomorrow and enter the park this evening for sunset for free; the evening does not use a pass day.

Buying online (angkorenterprise.gov.kh or the Angkor Pass app) is the official alternative: pick Mon 11 Jan as the start date, upload a plain-background photo without glasses, and the QR code arrives by email.
Only angkorenterprise.gov.kh, the app, the kiosks and the Road 60 office sell valid tickets. Do not buy from resellers.
Keep the pass on you all day: it is scanned at the road checkpoints and at most temples.
stops.cost: 1-day US$37 · 3-day US$62 · 7-day US$72 (card or cash; ATM on site)
stops.from_previous: From the Old Market: tuk-tuk 10–15 min (about US$2–3 by Grab/PassApp), or walk 4.8 km (65 min)
stops.warning: With the default Chiang Mai flights you land at 16:55 or 18:45, after the 17:30 counter closing. Buy the 3-day pass online at angkorenterprise.gov.kh before 10 Jan (photo upload needed), dated to start Mon 11 Jan.

stops.name: Old Market (Psar Chas), riverside and dinner
stops.description: Psar Chas is the town's original covered market, built in the French colonial period near the Siem Reap river. By day it sells everything from dried fish and spices to silk scarves, silver and carvings; in the evening the food stalls and the streets around it fill up. Pub Street, The Lane and Alley West are a block away, with restaurants and bars, and the river path with its lit footbridges is a calm place to walk after dinner. It is a good first-night introduction to Siem Reap's easy-going pace.
tips: The inner market winds down around 18:00–19:00; come back by day (e.g. SR3) if you want to shop properly.
For Khmer food try fish amok, lok lak and num banh chok (rice noodles with green fish curry); Malis, Mahob and Chanrey Tree are well-known Khmer restaurants a short walk away.
Bargain at stalls (start around half the asking price, and smile).
Pub Street gets loud after 21:00; the riverside and Kandal Village (one block east) are quieter.
stops.hours: Market stalls ~07:00–19:00; restaurants and bars until late
stops.from_previous: From the balloon: tuk-tuk 15–20 min (7 km), about US$4–5

video.title: Siem Reap - Peaceful Morning Walk [4K, No Commentary]

days.title: Angkor Wat sunrise on foot, then east through the forest temples
days.summary: An early, long and memorable day. Walk out of town in the dark to Angkor Wat (about 7.5 km), watch the towers appear against the dawn sky, then explore the temple while most sunrise visitors leave for breakfast. Leave by the quiet east gate and walk through the forest to Ta Keo, Ta Prohm and Banteay Kdei, then lunch at Srah Srang. In the afternoon take a tuk-tuk for East Mebon and Pre Rup, and finish with sunset from Pre Rup.
notes: Changed: reordered to Angkor Wat → Ta Keo → Ta Prohm → Banteay Kdei/Srah Srang, because on foot this is a continuous line (Ta Keo is next to Ta Prohm's north gate, and Banteay Kdei is 600 m from Ta Prohm's east gate). The draft order would add about 3 km of backtracking.

Walking total to Srah Srang is about 20 km including walking inside the temples. Pre Rup, East Mebon and Banteay Samre are best by tuk-tuk (Pre Rup is 14 km from town). Arrange a pickup at Srah Srang the evening before, or use Grab/PassApp, which work on the main park roads.
Pass day 1 of 3. Sunrise 06:31, first colour from about 05:50; sunset 17:55.

Bakan (Angkor Wat's top level) is open today: it closes only on Buddhist holy days and on the afternoons of the 14th and 28th of each month. 11 Jan is not a holy day (new moon ~8 Jan, first-quarter holy day ~15 Jan).
If tired, cut in this order: Banteay Samre, East Mebon, then go back to town after Srah Srang lunch and skip the Pre Rup sunset.

stops.name: Angkor Wat at sunrise, then the temple itself
stops.description: Angkor Wat was built in the early 12th century by King Suryavarman II as a temple to Vishnu and probably his own tomb, and it is still the largest religious monument in the world. It faces west across a 190 m-wide moat; the classic sunrise view is from the two reflection pools inside the outer wall, with the five lotus-bud towers outlined against the sky. After sunrise, walk the first-floor galleries, which hold about 800 m of bas-reliefs (the Churning of the Ocean of Milk on the east side of the south gallery is the most famous), then climb to Bakan, the steep top level, for views over the forest. It is still an active Buddhist site, with monks and offerings in the cross-shaped Preah Poan galleries.
tips: Walking out: from the Old Market follow Charles de Gaulle Blvd north past the Angkor National Museum to the checkpoint at the moat's south-west corner, then along the moat to the west causeway: 7.5 km, about 1 h 35. Leave by 04:10. Wear a headlamp or reflective layer; the road has a wide shoulder but tuk-tuks speed past in the dark. If you stay north of town (near Raffles/Charles de Gaulle) it is 5–6 km.

In mid-January the sun rises well to the right (south) of the towers. Stand at the western edge of the left (north) pool for the classic towers-and-reflection shot; the right (south) pool has a similar view with fewer people.
Do not leave at 06:40 with the crowds: the galleries are almost empty from 07:00 to 08:30. Bakan opens around 07:40; shoulders and knees must be covered.
Breakfast: stalls opposite the west entrance and on the north side of the temple serve noodles, coffee and fruit (US$3–5).
stops.hours: Angkor Wat 05:00–18:00; Bakan (top level) ~07:40–17:00, open on Mon 11 Jan
stops.from_previous: On foot from the Old Market, 7.5 km, about 1 h 35 (or tuk-tuk 20 min, about US$5–8 one way before dawn)

video.title: ANGKOR WAT (Cambodia) | Largest Temple in the World | Full Tour & Documentary in 4K

stops.name: Ta Keo
stops.description: Ta Keo is a five-tower temple-mountain started around 1000 AD by King Jayavarman V and never finished: according to inscriptions it was struck by lightning, which was taken as a bad omen, and work stopped. Because the carving never began, it is the plainest temple in Angkor, made of huge, smoothly cut greenish sandstone blocks, which makes the scale and geometry stand out. The steep stairs up its five tiers lead to a central tower more than 20 m above the ground, with views across the forest. It is usually quiet even when Ta Prohm next door is crowded.
tips: The east stairs are the easiest climb (there is a wooden staircase on part of it); go slowly on the way down.
Take the forest dirt road from Angkor Wat's east gate rather than the main road: it is shaded and almost empty.
stops.from_previous: On foot from Angkor Wat's east gate: about 4.8 km by the forest track and road, 60 min

video.title: Ta Keo Temple - Angkor's Grandest Unfinished Masterpiece

stops.name: Ta Prohm
stops.description: Ta Prohm was founded in 1186 by King Jayavarman VII as a Buddhist monastery dedicated to his mother; an inscription says it once had over 12,000 residents. When restoration began, the French chose to leave much of it as it was found, so silk-cotton and strangler fig trees still grow out of its towers and walls, their roots pouring over the stone. Today you follow wooden walkways through collapsed courtyards and dark corridors; some areas are propped up by the Archaeological Survey of India, which is restoring it. It is famous from the film Tomb Raider and is one of the most atmospheric places at Angkor.
tips: Enter by the quiet north gate (a few minutes from Ta Keo) and leave by the east gate, which puts you 600 m from Banteay Kdei.
Midday is busy; the famous 'Tomb Raider' tree (inner east courtyard) has a queue for photos. Look for the less-photographed roots in the outer galleries instead.
Stick to the marked paths: several sections are fenced off because of falling stones.
stops.from_previous: On foot from Ta Keo: about 1.2 km to Ta Prohm's north gate, 15 min

video.title: Amazing abandoned temple with trees in the jungle of Cambodia | Ta Prohm Temple Walking Tour | 4K

stops.name: Banteay Kdei and Srah Srang (with lunch)
stops.description: Banteay Kdei ('Citadel of the Monks' Cells') is another late-12th-century Buddhist monastery by Jayavarman VII, built in the same Bayon style as Ta Prohm but more open and much quieter. You walk in a straight line through four enclosures, past face-towers on the gates, dancing apsara carvings and half-collapsed galleries with trees growing through them. Its east gate opens onto Srah Srang, the 'Royal Bath', a 700 m-long reservoir dug in the 10th century with a sandstone landing stage guarded by lions and nagas. Srah Srang is a calm place to rest by the water, and the food stalls opposite are the natural lunch stop.
tips: Walk through Banteay Kdei from west to east and come out directly at Srah Srang.
Lunch at the restaurants across the road from Srah Srang (rice and noodle dishes US$4–6); confirm prices before ordering.
Srah Srang is also a peaceful sunrise spot (open from 05:00) — an option for the last morning on Thu 14.
stops.from_previous: On foot from Ta Prohm's east gate: 600 m, 8 min

video.title: Banteay Kdei Temple Tour 4K - Siem Reap Cambodia 2023

stops.name: East Mebon
stops.description: East Mebon was dedicated in 953 AD by King Rajendravarman to Shiva and to his parents. It stood on an artificial island in the middle of the East Baray, a 7 km by 1.8 km reservoir that is now dry rice fields, and boats would have landed at its four sides. Life-size stone elephants stand on the corners of its terraces, and five brick towers with fine lintel carvings crown the top. It is spacious, warm-coloured and usually close to empty.
tips: Look for the elephants on the corners of the first and second terraces; the one at the south-west corner is the best preserved.
Walking from Srah Srang is possible (1.8 km to Pre Rup, then 1.5 km to East Mebon) but the road is open and hot: take the tuk-tuk.
stops.from_previous: Tuk-tuk from Srah Srang: 3.2 km, 10 min (pickup arranged for the afternoon, about US$10–15 including the ride back to town)
stops.image_credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China, CC0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AEast_Mebon_%289713398037%29.jpg

video.title: 4K | East Mebon Temple Walking tour | Mountain temple in the center of the East baray

stops.name: Banteay Samre
stops.description: Banteay Samre is a mid-12th-century Hindu temple from the same period as Angkor Wat, on the far side of the old East Baray. It was heavily restored by French archaeologists in the 1940s, so it is one of the most complete small temples in the park: raised walkways, sunken courtyards, a central tower and crisp carved lintels with scenes from the Ramayana. Its name refers to the Samré, a local people, and a legend about a cucumber-farming king. Few tour groups come this far, so it is usually peaceful in the late afternoon.
tips: Only worth it if you still have energy: it adds about 40 minutes of tuk-tuk riding.
The inner courtyard is surrounded by a raised gallery; walk the whole circuit for the best lintels.
stops.from_previous: Tuk-tuk from East Mebon: about 5 km, 12 min
stops.image_credit: Photo Dharma from Penang, Malaysia, CC BY 2.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Banteay_Samre_-_001_Buildings_%288584547430%29.jpg

video.title: The Timeless Elegance of the Banteay Samre Temple, Siem Reap, Cambodia 2023

stops.name: Pre Rup at sunset
stops.description: Pre Rup was built in 961 AD by King Rajendravarman as his state temple, a pyramid of laterite and red brick with five towers on top. The name means 'turning the body', from a later belief that cremations took place here. At sunset the brick glows deep orange and you look west over rice fields and palm trees towards the forest, without the crowds of Phnom Bakheng. It is one of the best places for a quiet end to a long temple day.
tips: Climb to the top level by 17:20 to get a good spot on the west side; the sun sets at about 17:55.
Stairs are steep and narrow; bring a phone light for the way down after sunset.
Ask your tuk-tuk to wait at the east entrance car park, then ride 14 km (25 min) back to town.
stops.from_previous: Tuk-tuk from Banteay Samre: about 6 km, 15 min (or 1.3 km from East Mebon, 3 min)

video.title: AMAZING SUNSET VIEWS at Angkor Wat | Pre Rup Temple

days.title: Off-temple day: countryside, museum and the stilt village
days.summary: A rest from temples that still fills the day. Ride a quad through red-dirt village tracks and rice fields in the cool of the morning, spend late morning in the air-conditioned Angkor National Museum to put the temples in context, then drive an hour east to Kompong Khleang, the largest stilt-house town on the Tonle Sap lake, and take a boat out to the floating houses and open water for the late-afternoon light.
notes: No Angkor pass is needed today unless you choose Phnom Krom (which would use pass day 2 of 3).

Kompong Khleang and Phnom Krom are on opposite sides of town (about 85 min apart by car), so choose one for the afternoon. Kompong Khleang is the more unusual experience; Phnom Krom is the easier, shorter half-day with a sunset over the lake.
Traveler prefers unguided: the quad ride always has a lead rider (you cannot go alone), but Kompong Khleang works fine with just a hired car and the village boat — no guide needed.
If tired: skip the quad and sleep in after yesterday's 04:00 start; start with the museum at 08:30 instead.

stops.name: Quad bike ride through the countryside
stops.description: Several operators run guided quad (ATV) rides from bases on the edge of town into the countryside south and west of Siem Reap. You ride your own quad behind a lead rider along dirt tracks between rice paddies, palm-sugar trees, small pagodas and wooden stilt houses, with stops to see village life. In January the fields are harvested and golden and the tracks are dry and dusty. The oldest operator, Quad Adventure Cambodia, has morning departures at 07:00–07:30, and the cool early hours are the most pleasant time to ride.
tips: Quad Adventure Cambodia (since 2006): 'Discovery' 2 h 15 at 07:30 or 'Explorer' 3 h at 07:30; free hotel pickup; cash only (USD/riel). Book 1–2 days ahead via their website or WhatsApp.
Expect about US$50–80 for a 2-hour solo ride; private 2-hour tours via booking sites run US$120+.
Wear long trousers, closed shoes and sunglasses, and take a scarf or buff for the dust (masks are usually provided).
Unguided alternative: rent a bicycle (US$3–6) and ride the quiet roads along the Siem Reap river south to Wat Athvea and the rice fields.
stops.cost: About US$50–80 per rider for 2–3 h (not covered by the Angkor pass)
stops.from_previous: Free hotel pickup by the operator (10–15 min)

video.title: ATV with Cambodia Quadbike. Siem Reap

stops.warning: Prices are not published online; confirm the price and the 07:30 slot when booking.

stops.name: Angkor National Museum
stops.description: Opened in 2007 on the road to the temples, the museum explains the Khmer Empire and how Angkor was built, using statues and carvings brought in from the temples for safekeeping. Highlights are the Hall of a Thousand Buddhas, with rows of small Buddha images from different periods, and galleries on the kings Jayavarman VII and Suryavarman II, on religion, and on Angkor Wat. Short films and clear English labels make it a good place to understand what you saw yesterday and will see tomorrow. It is cool and quiet, ideal for the late-morning heat.
tips: Start with the short introductory film; it sets out the whole timeline.
The audio guide is worth renting if you like detail (extra cost at the desk).
Photography is not allowed in most galleries.
Lunch: the museum café, or the restaurants on Charles de Gaulle Blvd and Sivatha Blvd nearby.
stops.from_previous: Operator drops you at the hotel; then tuk-tuk 5 min (2 km, about US$1.50–2) or walk 25 min from the Old Market

video.title: Angkor National Museum Siem Reap Cambodia

stops.name: Kompong Khleang stilt village and Tonle Sap boat
stops.description: Kompong Khleang is the largest settlement on the Tonle Sap lake: a working fishing town of around 1,000 families whose wooden houses stand on stilts up to 8–10 m tall, with schools, pagodas and a market, and a floating section of houseboats further out on the lake. The lake rises and falls by several metres each year; in January the water is high to medium, so the boat can still run along the main channel between the stilt houses and out to the floating village and the open lake. Unlike Chong Kneas and Kampong Phluk, it sees few tourists, so it feels like a real town rather than a show. A late-afternoon boat gives warm light on the houses and, from the lake edge, sunset over the water.
tips: Go unguided: hire a car and driver for the afternoon (about US$35–60 return; 75–90 min each way) — a tuk-tuk takes about 2 h each way and is dusty.
Buy the boat at the jetty: about US$20–25 per person (no posted price, agree before boarding); 1–1.5 h through the village to the floating houses and the lake.
Ask the boatman to stop so you can also walk the stilt-house street and the pagoda; there are few toilets, so plan ahead.
Stay on the lake for sunset (~17:55) if your driver agrees to a later return; bring repellent for dusk.
stops.hours: Village always open; boats run in daylight (roughly 07:00–18:00)
stops.cost: Boat US$20–25 per person; car and driver US$35–60 return; not on the Angkor pass
stops.from_previous: Car from the museum: 52 km, 75–90 min via National Road 6 and Dam Dek

video.title: Siem Reap's BEST Kept Secret Kompong Khleang Floating Village 4K

stops.warning: Boat prices are negotiated; a few 2025 visitors were charged a US$15 village entry when arriving without a boat booking.

stops.name: Phnom Krom sunset (alternative to Kompong Khleang)
stops.description: Phnom Krom is a 140 m hill 12 km south of town, right at the edge of the Tonle Sap. On top stand three late-9th-century sandstone towers built by King Yasovarman I to Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma, next to a working pagoda. From the summit you look over flooded fields, the Chong Kneas floating village and the lake, and the sun sets over the water. It is quiet compared with Phnom Bakheng and an easy half-day if you skip Kompong Khleang.
tips: Ride up by tuk-tuk (the road goes to the top) or climb the ~300 steps from the bottom.
Stop at Wat Athvea, a quiet 12th-century temple, on the way (5 km south of town).
Your pass is checked at the top, so this would use one of your 3 pass days.
stops.cost: Angkor pass (3-day pass, US$62) — pass checked at the summit
stops.from_previous: Tuk-tuk from town: 12 km, 25–30 min (about US$10–12 return with waiting)

video.title: 【4K】PHNOM KROM / Cambodia - Virtual Tour - Trip to Siem Reap

days.title: Angkor Thom and the Grand Circuit by e-bike
days.summary: A full day on two wheels (about 45 km in total). Ride out past Angkor Wat to the South Gate of Angkor Thom, the walled royal city, walk a quiet stretch of its 8 m-high wall, then see the stone faces of the Bayon, the Baphuon and the royal terraces with their hidden inner walls. After lunch, leave by the North Gate for the Grand Circuit temples of Preah Khan, Neak Pean and Ta Som, then ride back to climb Phnom Bakheng for sunset.
notes: Changed: the Angkor Balloon moved here from SR1 as an optional sunrise ride before the wall walk, because the Sunday flight lands too late for a sunset ride.
Pass day 2 of 3. Sunrise 06:31, sunset 17:55.
Changed: the Angkor Thom wall walk moves to the start of the day, at the South Gate (where you enter anyway), so you walk it in the cool early morning instead of doubling back later.

Distances by bike: town → South Gate 8.8 km; South Gate → Bayon 1.7 km; Bayon area → North Gate 1–2 km; North Gate → Preah Khan 2.6 km; Preah Khan → Neak Pean 2.7 km; Neak Pean → Ta Som 2.2 km; Ta Som → Phnom Bakheng about 11 km (back via Preah Khan and through Angkor Thom); Bakheng → town 9 km. Total about 42–45 km, plus about 3 km on the wall.
An e-bike is strongly recommended over a pedal bike for this distance in 32°C heat; check its range covers 50 km or note where the rental company's charging points are.

Phnom Bakheng allows only about 300 people at the summit at a time. Be at the base by 16:00–16:15. If the queue is too long, watch sunset from the South Gate causeway or the SW corner of the Angkor Thom wall instead.
If tired: cut the wall walk first, then Ta Som; Neak Pean is a 15-minute stop.

stops.name: Angkor Balloon at sunrise
stops.description: A tethered helium balloon that rises about 120–200 m on a cable from a field just west of Angkor Wat's moat and hangs there for 10–15 minutes. From the basket you see the five towers of Angkor Wat rising out of the forest inside their square moat, Phnom Bakheng on its hill, the West Baray reservoir and, on clear evenings, the Tonle Sap lake. It is a short, simple ride, not a hot-air balloon flight, but it is the only easy bird's-eye view of Angkor Wat. The launch site is outside the temple checkpoints, so no pass is needed.
tips: Look for the yellow balloon over the trees as you ride out: if it is not up, it is probably not flying (wind).
At sunrise the sun comes up behind Angkor Wat, so you see the towers in silhouette with the forest glowing; it is calm and nearly empty at this hour.
From the launch field it is about 3 km by e-bike to the South Gate of Angkor Thom for the wall walk.
Do not confuse it with the hot-air balloon tours sold online, which are a different company and fly from the countryside.
stops.hours: Sundays 05:15–18:15 (weekday hours are shorter); flights only in calm weather
stops.from_previous: From town: e-bike or tuk-tuk 15–20 min (about 6 km)

video.title: Riding a Hot Air Balloon Over Angkor Wat

stops.warning: The most recent reviews found are from late 2024; confirm it is operating (ask your hotel or tuk-tuk driver) before planning around it.

stops.name: Angkor Thom South Gate and wall walk
stops.description: Angkor Thom ('Great City') was the last capital of the Khmer Empire, built by Jayavarman VII in the late 12th century and enclosed by a 3 km-square wall 8 m high and a wide moat. The South Gate causeway is lined with 54 gods and 54 demons holding a giant naga serpent, leading to a 23 m gate tower topped by four huge faces. A shaded dirt path runs along the top of the wall: from the South Gate it is about 1.5 km west to the small south-west corner shrine, Prasat Chrung, with views over the moat. Very few visitors walk up here, so it feels like a private forest path.
tips: Get on the wall from inside the South Gate: pass through the gate, and the path up is on the left (west) side, a short slope.
Walk (or push the bike) 1.5 km to the SW Prasat Chrung and back: about 1 h. Motorbikes are banned on the wall since 2021; bicycles are allowed.
Stop on the causeway before the gate early, before the tour buses (from about 08:30), for photos of the gods and demons.
The North Gate, Victory Gate and Gate of the Dead (east side) are also quiet; you pass the North Gate later today.
stops.hours: Park hours (about 05:00–18:30); the wall path has no gate
stops.from_previous: From the balloon field: about 3 km north by e-bike past Angkor Wat to the South Gate (10–15 min). E-bike from town via Angkor Wat: 8.8 km, 35–40 min

video.title: SECRET Angkor Thom wall walk! 5 ancient gates! Stunning views! Siem Reap, Cambodia, 2023!

stops.name: Bayon
stops.description: The Bayon stands at the exact centre of Angkor Thom and was Jayavarman VII's state temple, built around 1200 as a Buddhist temple. Its upper terrace is a crowded forest of 37 surviving towers carrying more than 200 huge, calmly smiling stone faces, usually thought to show the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, the king, or both. The outer gallery has some of Angkor's best bas-reliefs, showing not only battles with the Cham navy but everyday life: markets, cooking, cockfights and a woman giving birth. Its maze-like layout means every corner gives a new arrangement of faces.
tips: Walk the outer gallery first (east side, then clockwise along the south side) for the everyday-life reliefs, then go up to the faces.
The upper terrace is best before 10:00, before the heat and the groups; the faces are lit from the east in the morning.
Park the bike at the stands on the north side; vendors will watch it for a tip.
stops.from_previous: E-bike from the South Gate: 1.7 km, 7 min

video.title: 4K Bayon Temple Walking Tour | Amazing temple in the center of Angkor Thom

stops.name: Baphuon, Phimeanakas and Preah Palilay
stops.description: Baphuon is an 11th-century temple-mountain reached by a 200 m raised walkway on short columns. French archaeologists took it apart in the 1960s to rebuild it, the records were lost during the Khmer Rouge years, and it was finally reassembled like a 300,000-piece jigsaw, reopening in 2011. Its west side was rebuilt in the 16th century as a huge reclining Buddha, which you can still make out. Behind it, inside the old royal palace grounds, is Phimeanakas, a small, steep pyramid that was the king's temple, and in the forest to the north, Preah Palilay, a lonely tree-shaded sanctuary with fine Buddhist carvings.
tips: Baphuon's top level needs covered shoulders and knees and has steep stairs; the view over the treetops is worth it.
Walk around to the west side of Baphuon to see the outline of the reclining Buddha.
From Phimeanakas, follow the path north through the palace grounds (past the royal pools) to Preah Palilay and Tep Pranam.
stops.hours: 06:00–18:30 (2026 schedule; Baphuon's upper level may close earlier)
stops.from_previous: On foot from the Bayon: 400 m, 6 min (leave the bike or push it)

stops.name: Terrace of the Elephants and Terrace of the Leper King (with hidden inner walls)
stops.description: The Terrace of the Elephants is a 350 m-long royal viewing platform in front of the palace, where the king watched parades; its wall is carved with near life-size elephants and hunting scenes. At its north end stands the Terrace of the Leper King, named after a statue whose lichen-covered surface looked like leprosy (the original is now in the National Museum in Phnom Penh). The secret here is the 'hidden wall': when French restorers rebuilt the outer wall they found an older, inner wall behind it, and you can walk along the narrow trench between them past rows of almost untouched carvings of nagas, kings, apsaras and sea creatures. A similar hidden inner wall with a five-headed horse sits at the north end of the Elephant Terrace.
tips: The entrance to the Leper King's inner wall passage is at the south-front corner of the terrace: follow the narrow gap that zig-zags behind the outer wall.
For the Elephant Terrace inner wall, look for the small passage at the terrace's north stairway (five-headed horse relief).
The trench is shaded and cool — a good midday stop.
Lunch: stalls and small restaurants across the road from the terraces (US$4–6).
stops.from_previous: On foot from Preah Palilay: 400 m, 5 min
stops.image_credit: Jorge Láscar from Australia, CC BY 2.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ATerrace_of_the_Leper_King_%286208375256%29.jpg
