stops.name: Preah Khan
stops.description: Preah Khan ('Sacred Sword') was built by Jayavarman VII in 1191 on the site of a victory over the Cham, and dedicated to his father. It was a huge monastery and teaching centre with over 1,000 teachers, and its long, straight corridors with hundreds of doorways in a row are its signature view. Parts are restored and parts are left in a romantic state of collapse, with trees on the walls, as at Ta Prohm, but with far fewer people. Look for the unusual two-storey building with round columns, which looks almost Greek, and the 'Hall of Dancers' carved with apsaras.
tips: Enter by the west gate (approach road with a giant garuda on the wall) and walk the main corridor east; have the bike collected or push it round to the east gate.
The central stupa replaced a statue of the Buddha; look for the chiselled-out Buddha images, defaced during a Hindu revival in the 13th century.
stops.from_previous: E-bike from the terraces through the North Gate: about 3.7 km, 15 min

video.title: Walking Tour of Preah Khan Temple in the Jungle | Temple complex of Angkor, Cambodia | 4K

stops.name: Neak Pean
stops.description: Neak Pean ('Entwined Serpents') is a small 12th-century shrine on a round island in the middle of a square pool, in what was once the middle of a large reservoir. It represents Lake Anavatapta in the Himalayas, whose waters were believed to cure illness; four smaller pools around it are fed through spouts shaped as an elephant, a lion, a horse and a human head. Pilgrims came to bathe here for healing. You reach it on a long wooden boardwalk across a lake full of dead trees, which is part of the atmosphere.
tips: You cannot enter the pools; the best view is from the platform at the end of the boardwalk.
In January the reservoir usually still has water around the boardwalk, giving good reflections.
stops.from_previous: E-bike from Preah Khan's east side: 2.7 km, 10 min

stops.name: Ta Som
stops.description: Ta Som is a small temple built by Jayavarman VII in the late 12th century, with Bayon-style face towers on its gates. Its famous sight is the eastern gate, almost swallowed by a huge strangler fig whose roots frame the stone face. Inside are quiet, crumbling galleries with well-preserved devata (female deity) carvings. It has the jungle-ruin feel of Ta Prohm with a fraction of the visitors.
tips: Walk straight through to the east gate for the tree-gate view, best seen from outside the gate looking back.
This is the turnaround point: from here ride back west the way you came for Phnom Bakheng (about 11 km, 40 min).
stops.from_previous: E-bike from Neak Pean: 2.2 km, 8 min

stops.name: Phnom Bakheng at sunset
stops.description: Phnom Bakheng is the oldest temple-mountain of the Angkor capital, built around 900 AD by King Yasovarman I on a natural hill as the centre of his city, Yasodharapura. Its five-tiered pyramid once carried 108 small towers, a number full of cosmic meaning. From the top you see Angkor Wat's towers in the forest to the south-east, the West Baray shining to the west and plains stretching to the horizon. It has been the classic sunset spot for over a century, which is why numbers at the top are now limited.
tips: Walk up the zig-zag path on the east side (about 15–20 min); the old elephant rides have ended.
Only about 300 people are allowed on the summit at once; staff count you in. Arriving at the base by 16:00–16:15 normally gets you up; later you may queue until people leave.
Angkor Wat is seen side-on in the evening light; the real show is the sun going down over the West Baray (~17:55).
Guards clear the summit about 20 minutes before closing; you will ride the 9 km back to town in the dark — make sure the e-bike lights work.
stops.hours: 05:00–19:00 (sunset site); summit capacity about 300 people at a time
stops.from_previous: E-bike from Ta Som: about 11 km back via Preah Khan, the North Gate and through Angkor Thom to the South Gate, 40–45 min

video.title: Sunset from Phnom Bakheng - 9th Century Khmer Temple - Angkor Cambodia 2024

stops.warning: Summit capacity is capped (about 300); arrive at the base by 16:15.

days.title: Last sunrise and departure
days.summary: If your flight leaves after about midday, use the third pass day for a quiet sunrise at Srah Srang and an early, nearly empty Ta Prohm, then head to the airport about three hours before departure. With an early flight, just allow about 1 h for the drive and 2 h at the airport.
notes: SAI is 47 km from town: allow 50–60 min by car, and arrive 2 h before an international flight. Leave town about 3 h before departure.
Pass day 3 of 3 (if not used on Tue for Phnom Krom). Thu 14 Jan: Bakan at Angkor Wat closes from 13:00 (the 14th of every month), which does not affect this plan.
Book your airport car or the shuttle the day before; Grab drivers may refuse the long airport run early in the morning.

stops.name: Sunrise at Srah Srang, then Ta Prohm at opening
stops.description: Srah Srang, the 10th-century royal bathing reservoir opposite Banteay Kdei, is a much calmer sunrise spot than Angkor Wat: the sun comes up over the far end of the water, behind palms, with the lion-guarded landing stage in the foreground. Afterwards, Ta Prohm is 1 km away and is at its best in the first hour after opening, in soft light and with few people, before the sunrise groups arrive. It is a peaceful last look at Angkor before you leave.
tips: Tuk-tuk from town: 25 min (14 km) — about US$12–15 for the pickup, waiting and return by 08:30.
Sit on the stone landing stage; the sun appears around 06:31.
No pass day left? Walk to Wat Bo pagoda's murals and the quiet lanes of Kandal Village, or the local Psar Leu market, instead.
stops.hours: Srah Srang 05:00–19:00; Ta Prohm from 06:00 (2026 schedule)
stops.from_previous: Tuk-tuk from town: 14 km, 25 min

stops.name: Transfer to Siem Reap Angkor International Airport (SAI)
stops.time: Leave town ~3 h before your flight
stops.description: The drive back to SAI takes 50–60 minutes on the new road east through rice fields. The terminal is modern and quiet, with cafés and duty-free; check-in for international flights usually opens 2–3 hours before departure. Spend the last riel at the airport or give it away: it is hard to change outside Cambodia.
tips: Airport shuttle bus from the CDF Duty Free stop near Wat Bo: US$8, about 60–70 min; departures to the airport (early-2025 timetable) 05:30, 07:00, 08:00, 10:00, 12:00, 13:30, 16:00, 17:30, 19:00 — check the current times.
Hotel car or taxi: US$25–35; book the day before.
Confirm whether your onward country needs an arrival form (e.g. Thailand's TDAC, Malaysia's MDAC).
stops.from_previous: Car from town: 47 km, 50–60 min

backup_ideas.name: Amazing Thailand Countdown 2027 at ICONSIAM
backup_ideas.note: great, but i get IN on the 1st, so not sure if thats too late for part of the festival
backup_ideas.blurb: Bangkok's biggest New Year celebration runs as a five-day festival at ICONSIAM's River Park with concerts and drone shows, ending with a 1,400 m fireworks display along the Chao Phraya at midnight on 31 December. Watch from the river park, a rooftop, a riverside hotel or a dinner cruise.

backup_ideas.name: Khao Sok: Cheow Lan Lake floating bungalows
backup_ideas.blurb: An emerald reservoir inside one of the world's oldest rainforests, ringed by sheer limestone karsts. Sleep in a bamboo raft house on the water, kayak at dawn while gibbons call, swim off your porch, and hike to jungle caves such as Nam Talu.

backup_ideas.name: Overnight sleeper train Bangkok → Chiang Mai
backup_ideas.blurb: Thailand's classic rail journey on the Chinese-built sleeper cars (in service since 2016): staff make up your bunk after dinner, and you wake to the train climbing through teak forests and the Khun Tan tunnel into the northern hills. Upgrade option: the restored 1960s 'Blue Jasmine' train (launched Nov 2025) runs a 9-day luxury Bangkok–Chiang Mai journey with stops at Ayutthaya, Uthai Thani and Sukhothai.

backup_ideas.name: Bang Krachao by bike ('Bangkok's green lung')
backup_ideas.blurb: A jungle-covered loop of the Chao Phraya where 2 m-wide raised concrete paths wind through mangroves, banana groves and stilt villages. Rent a bike at the pier, ride to Sri Nakhon Khuean Khan Park with its lake and birdwatching tower, and stop at canal-side cafés; on weekends visit Bang Nam Phueng floating market.

backup_ideas.name: Bangkokian Museum
backup_ideas.blurb: A family's 1930s wooden house and garden kept exactly as it was, showing how a middle-class Bangkok household lived before the high-rises. Rooms of furniture, records, kitchenware and photos, plus a doctor's surgery building, all in a shady garden off Charoen Krung.

backup_ideas.name: Museum Siam
backup_ideas.blurb: A modern, interactive museum in a grand colonial-era ministry building that asks 'what does it mean to be Thai?' through playful rooms on history, food, beliefs and identity. In 2026–27 it is also a Bangkok Art Biennale venue with contemporary installations.

backup_ideas.name: Ban Tawai woodcarving village
backup_ideas.blurb: A long-established crafts village of open workshops where carvers make Lanna-style wood carvings, furniture and lacquerware. Walk the lanes and watch the artisans at work; it pairs well with Wat Inthrawat nearby.

backup_ideas.name: Bo Sang umbrella village & Umbrella Festival
backup_ideas.blurb: Bo Sang is the home of hand-painted paper and cotton umbrellas; workshops show every step from bamboo frame to painting. During the festival the village street is hung with hundreds of umbrellas, with parades, crafts and a 'Miss Bo Sang' on bicycles holding umbrellas. Nearby San Kamphaeng has silk and celadon workshops and the MAIIAM contemporary art museum.

backup_ideas.name: Huai Nam Dang: Doi Kiew Lom sea of mist & Pong Duet hot springs
backup_ideas.blurb: Doi Kiew Lom viewpoint at the park headquarters looks over rolling ridges toward Doi Luang Chiang Dao, and in the cool season the valleys fill with a sea of mist at dawn. On the way back, Pong Duet has boiling geysers and natural hot pools in the forest for a soak.

backup_ideas.name: Huay Tung Tao Lake
backup_ideas.blurb: A reservoir at the foot of Doi Suthep lined with bamboo huts on stilts where you lounge over the water and order grilled fish, som tam and cold drinks. Giant straw sculptures sit around the lake, and a paved loop is good for a bike ride or short walk.

backup_ideas.name: Warorot Market & Ton Lam Yai flower market
backup_ideas.blurb: Chiang Mai's main local market (Kad Luang): three floors of northern sausages, chili pastes, dried fruit, hill-tribe textiles and household goods. Across the street, Ton Lam Yai flower market is busiest at night with marigold garlands for the temples.

backup_ideas.name: Wat Inthrawat (Wat Ton Kwen)
backup_ideas.blurb: A small, carefully preserved 1850s Lanna temple in a village setting: a teak wihan with sweeping layered roofs and a rare open-sided pavilion (mondop) that once sheltered a Buddha relic during processions. It is regarded as one of the best examples of original Lanna wooden architecture left.

backup_ideas.name: Wiang Kum Kam ancient city
backup_ideas.blurb: The first capital of King Mengrai (late 1200s), abandoned after floods and buried under river silt until the 1980s. More than 20 excavated temple ruins sit among village lanes and rice fields; you explore by bicycle, horse cart or small tram, stopping at Wat Chedi Liam (a working temple with a stepped Mon-style chedi) and Wat Kan Thom.

backup_ideas.name: Phnom Kulen
backup_ideas.blurb: The mountain where Jayavarman II declared the Khmer Empire in 802 AD. Visit carved riverbed lingas, the 16th-century reclining Buddha on top of a boulder at Preah Ang Thom, and swim at the two-level waterfall; with a motorbike guide you can reach forest-covered temples like Prasat Rong Chen.

backup_ideas.name: Kampot & Kep (with the Phnom Penh–Kampot train)
backup_ideas.blurb: Kampot is a sleepy riverside town of faded French shophouses, sunset river cruises and Kampot pepper farms. Above it, Bokor Mountain holds an abandoned 1920s French hill station with a ghostly church and palace hotel; nearby Kep is a seaside village known for crab fresh from the market and boats to Rabbit Island.

backup_ideas.name: Kuching & Bako (Malaysian Borneo)
backup_ideas.blurb: A relaxed riverside city with a white-rajah history, Chinese temples and colonial forts. From here you can see semi-wild orangutans at Semenggoh, hike the coastal jungle of Bako National Park to spot proboscis monkeys, and visit a Bidayuh longhouse at Annah Rais.

backup_ideas.name: Nan (northern Thailand)
backup_ideas.blurb: A sleepy, old Lanna-era city in a green valley, famous for the 19th-century murals of Wat Phumin (including the 'whispering' couple) and the gold chedi of Wat Phra That Chae Haeng. Rent a scooter or hire a driver for the Sapan village rice terraces, the ancient Bo Kluea mountain salt wells and the sea-of-fog viewpoint at Doi Samer Dao.

backup_ideas.name: Penang: George Town
backup_ideas.blurb: A UNESCO-listed trading port of Chinese clan houses, Peranakan mansions, mosques, Hindu temples and colonial streets, all walkable. Explore the Khoo Kongsi clan temple and the clan jetties on stilts, eat at the hawker stalls (Penang is Malaysia's food capital), ride the funicular up Penang Hill and visit the huge Kek Lok Si temple.
